title: SPARK CSEC Physics - Paper 01 Practice Paper 1
subject: Physics
syllabus: CXC 22/G/SYLL 13, for examinations from May and June 2015
instructions: This test consists of 60 items. You will have 1 hour and 15 minutes to answer them.
In addition to this test booklet, you should have an answer sheet.
Each item in this test has four suggested answers lettered (A), (B), (C), (D). Read each item you are about to answer and decide which choice is best.
On your answer sheet, find the number which corresponds to your item and shade the space having the same letter as the answer you have chosen.
If you want to change your answer, erase it completely before you fill in your new choice.
When you are told to begin, turn the page and work as quickly and as carefully as you can. If you cannot answer an item, go on to the next one. You may return to that item later.
You may do any rough work in this booklet.
Figures are not necessarily drawn to scale.
You may use a silent, non-programmable calculator to answer items.

items.objective_statement: investigate the factors which might affect the period of a simple pendulum
items.stem: Which change increases the period of a simple pendulum?

misconception.label: Mass does not appear in the formula and has no effect.

options.text: Increasing the length of the string

misconception.label: For small angles the period does not change with the angle of swing.
The thickness of the string is not a factor.

steps: The period depends on the length alone, through T = 2π√(l/g).
solution.answer_line: Increasing the length of the string

items.objective_statement: discuss possible types and sources of error in any measurement
items.stem: A voltmeter reads 0.2 V when nothing is connected to it. Every later reading is therefore too large by 0.2 V. This is an example of

misconception.label: Parallax comes from reading a scale at an angle, and it varies.
An anomalous result is a single reading that does not fit the pattern.
A random error changes size and direction from reading to reading.

steps: The same error appears in every reading, in the same direction, which is what makes it systematic.
solution.answer_line: a systematic error

items.stem: Which of the following is a vector quantity?

items.objective_statement: define the moment of a force, T
items.stem: The moment of a force about a point is defined as the force multiplied by

options.text: the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force
the distance moved in the direction of the force

misconception.label: Force times distance moved is work, measured in joules.
Mass plays no part in a moment.

steps: That perpendicular distance is what the definition requires, and its omission is the commonest lost mark in the topic.

items.stem: For the beam to balance, the weight W, in N, must be

misconception.label: Divided by the wrong distance.
Assumed the weights must be equal, ignoring the distances.
Multiplied by the ratio of the distances instead of dividing.

items.stem: The point P on the graph is the

misconception.label: Confused the limit of proportionality with the elastic limit, which lies a little beyond it.

options.text: limit of proportionality of the spring
point at which the spring breaks

misconception.label: A break would end the graph, not bend it.

misconception.label: Divided the time by the velocity instead of the velocity by the time.
Read the time taken rather than the acceleration.

items.stem: The total distance travelled in the 30 s, in m, is

misconception.label: Counted only the rectangle and one triangle.
Used the whole time at the top speed for one of the sloping parts.
Treated the whole shape as a rectangle 30 s by 20 m s⁻¹.

steps: The distance travelled is the area under a velocity-time graph.
Accelerating: ½ × 10 × 20 = 100 m. At constant speed: 10 × 20 = 200 m. Slowing: ½ × 10 × 20 = 100 m.

items.objective_statement: define linear momentum
items.stem: The unit of linear momentum may be written as

misconception.label: N/kg is gravitational field strength.
J s is not a unit used in this syllabus.
kg m/s² is the newton, the unit of force.

steps: Momentum is mass times velocity, so kg × m/s. This is also the newton second.
solution.answer_line: kg m/s

items.objective_statement: describe situations that demonstrate the law of conservation of linear momentum
items.stem: When a rifle is fired, it recoils backwards because

misconception.label: The explosion pushes both ways.

options.text: the bullet pushes the air backwards

misconception.label: The air is not the reason for recoil.

options.text: the total momentum before and after firing must remain zero
the rifle is heavier than the bullet

misconception.label: The mass difference explains the speed of the recoil, not its cause.

steps: Momentum is conserved, so the forward momentum of the bullet must be matched by an equal backward momentum of the rifle.
solution.answer_line: the total momentum before and after firing must remain zero

items.objective_statement: apply Archimedes’ principle to predict whether a body would float or sink in a given fluid
items.stem: A body floats in a liquid. The upthrust on it is equal to

options.text: the weight of the body plus the weight of liquid displaced

misconception.label: This counts the same force twice.
A volume is not a force and cannot balance a weight.
A density is not a force either.

steps: A floating body is in equilibrium, so the upthrust balances its weight. By Archimedes' principle that upthrust is also the weight of liquid displaced.
solution.answer_line: the weight of the body

stimulus.label: Item 22 refers to the following graph, which shows how the temperature of a solid changes as it is heated at a steady rate.
stimulus.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 340 238" width="100%" style="max-width:340px;height:auto;color:inherit" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12"><path d="M54 192 L312 192"/><path d="M312 192 L305.0 189.1 L305.0 194.9 Z" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><path d="M54 192 L54 34"/><path d="M54 34 L51.1 41.0 L56.9 41.0 Z" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><path d="M54 168 L114 106 L204 106 L270 52" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M54 106 L114 106" stroke-width="0.8" stroke-dasharray="4 3" opacity="0.65"/><text x="159" y="94" text-anchor="middle" stroke="none" fill="currentColor" font-size="12">Q</text><text x="183" y="222" text-anchor="middle" stroke="none" fill="currentColor" font-size="12">Time</text><text transform="rotate(-90 18 113)" x="18" y="113" text-anchor="middle" stroke="none" fill="currentColor" font-size="12">Temperature</text></svg>
stimulus.alt: A graph of temperature against time for a solid being heated steadily. The temperature rises, stays constant along a flat section labelled Q, then rises again.

items.stem: During the part of the graph labelled Q, the energy supplied is used to

options.text: raise the temperature of the solid

misconception.label: The temperature is constant along Q, so it is not being raised.

options.text: break the forces holding the particles in the solid together
raise the temperature of the liquid formed

misconception.label: The liquid warms only after the melting is complete, beyond Q.

options.text: increase the average speed of the particles

misconception.label: The average speed of the particles is fixed by the temperature, which is constant here.

steps: Along Q the temperature does not change even though energy is still being supplied.
Energy supplied without a temperature rise is latent heat.
It is used to break the forces holding the particles in their fixed positions, so the solid melts.
solution.answer_line: break the forces holding the particles in the solid together

items.objective_statement: recall that the decay process is independent of the conditions external to the nucleus
items.stem: The rate of decay of a radioactive isotope is unaffected by

options.text: the number of undecayed nuclei present

misconception.label: The rate does depend on how many nuclei remain.
Different isotopes decay at very different rates.
The half-life is a property of the isotope and determines the rate.

steps: Decay is a nuclear process, so external conditions such as temperature, pressure and chemical state have no effect on it.
solution.answer_line: the temperature of the sample

items.objective_statement: solve problems involving half-life

stimulus.label: Item 59 refers to the following graph, which shows how the count rate from a radioactive source falls with time.
stimulus.alt: A decay curve of count rate against time, falling from 80 counts per second and halving every 10 seconds.

items.stem: The half-life of the source, in s, is

misconception.label: Halved the time taken rather than reading it from the graph.
Read the time for the count rate to fall to a quarter, which is two half-lives.
Read the whole time shown on the graph.

steps: The half-life is the time for the count rate to fall to half its value.
From the graph the count rate is 80 at the start and 40 after 10 s.
The half-life is therefore 10 s, and the next fall, 40 to 20, takes the same 10 s.

items.stem: The energy released in a nuclear reaction comes from

misconception.label: Chemical bonds are not involved in nuclear reactions.

options.text: the movement of electrons between shells

misconception.label: Electron transitions release far less energy.
No burning takes place.

options.text: a small loss of mass converted into energy

steps: The products have slightly less mass than the reactants, and E = mc squared converts that difference into a very large energy.
solution.answer_line: a small loss of mass converted into energy
